Novel tooling applied to the same work is not a new business capability; calling it transformation inflates the claim.

Correct. Efficiency is precisely this shape: identical defined work delivered at lower cost and faster cycle time, with the 70% unit-cost drop as the headline metric. Naming the pillar accurately matters because it sets which measurements the executive readout should anchor on and what expectations follow.

Tempting because staff leverage sounds like the human framing of the same numbers, but productivity as a pillar means people accomplish more or higher-value output. Here output is fixed and the machine absorbed the work — the gain is in cost and speed of the process, not in expanded human accomplishment.

Faster turnaround is real, but 'performance' as a pillar concerns meeting defined SLAs and service commitments, and the stem states no SLA target being met or missed. Turnaround here is one component of the efficiency story, not a distinct pillar being served.
principle: efficiency is the same work done cheaper and faster; name the pillar the numbers actually support
relatedConcept: Classifying a design's value pillar correctly determines which metrics prove success and keeps executive expectations honest.

objective: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
question: A telehealth platform is contractually bound to answer patients' routine pre-visit questions with a p95 response under 3 seconds; breaches carry financial penalties. The architecture team's favored design uses Opus with a rich multi-step retrieval flow, benchmarking at 6-to-9-second responses of excellent quality. Patient testing shows a faster, slightly less polished answer is preferred anyway. What should the architect direct?
options: Ship the Opus design and renegotiate the SLA, since demonstrably superior answer quality justifies revisiting the contract terms
Ship the Opus design with an animated progress indicator, since perceived latency matters more to patients than measured latency
Run the Opus flow asynchronously and deliver answers by notification, converting the interaction so the 3-second bound no longer applies
Rework the design around the SLA: a faster model with a single-pass retrieval flow engineered to meet the p95 bound, quality-checked against the contract's scope of routine questions
optionExplanations: Tempting because the quality is real, but it treats a binding constraint as negotiable on the vendor's preferred timeline while penalties accrue. Contracted SLAs are design inputs, not outputs — proposing renegotiation is a business conversation, not an architecture that meets the commitment.

Perceived-latency tricks improve waiting, but the contract binds measured p95, so penalties trigger regardless of how pleasant the spinner is. This confuses a UX mitigation with SLA compliance — the metric that carries financial consequences is unmoved.

Tempting because asynchrony genuinely sidesteps latency bounds for some workloads, but pre-visit Q&A is an interactive use case: patients are present and waiting, and the stem says they prefer fast answers. Redefining the interaction to dodge the SLA serves the architecture, not the patient or the contract.

Correct. The SLA is the requirement; the design must be derived from it, not defended against it. A faster model with a bounded single-pass flow can be engineered to the p95 target, and the stem confirms the quality trade is acceptable for routine questions — the performance pillar directs this choice, and patient preference corroborates it.
principle: SLAs are binding design constraints that drive model and pattern choices
relatedConcept: Performance-pillar alignment means engineering to the contracted metric first and optimizing quality within that envelope.
overallExplanation: SLAs are binding design constraints that drive model and pattern choices. Performance-pillar alignment means engineering to the contracted metric first and optimizing quality within that envelope.

objective: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
question: A manufacturing conglomerate's innovation lab requests architecture support for a multi-agent 'factory intelligence mesh' spanning maintenance, scheduling, and procurement. Asked what it improves, the sponsor says the company 'needs a flagship AI initiative' and competitors 'are doing agents.' No metric, owner, or affected process is identified. Six months of platform budget is at stake. How should the architect respond?
options: Design the mesh with strong observability baked in, so whichever benefits emerge after launch can be measured and reported credibly
Accept the initiative but descope it to a single-agent pilot in maintenance, cutting the investment while preserving the flagship story
Require the sponsor to identify a target process, an owner, a baseline, and a value pillar with a metric before any architecture work begins, and offer to facilitate that discovery
Benchmark the named competitors' agent deployments first, so the initiative's scope can be justified by documented industry practice
optionExplanations: Tempting because observability is a genuine virtue, but instrumenting an aimless system just measures aimlessness precisely. 'Launch, then discover the benefit' inverts the value discipline: without a target metric there is no way to design toward anything, and six months of budget is spent finding out what the question was.

Descoping reduces the waste but keeps the flawed premise: the pilot still has no metric, owner, or process problem it exists to move, so even its results will be uninterpretable. A smaller tech-led initiative is still tech-led — the missing ingredient is a value case, not a smaller blast radius.

Correct. Architecture that cannot name the value pillar it serves and the metric it will move is not ready to be designed. Insisting on a target process, baseline, owner, and measurable outcome converts a fashion-driven request into a fundable case — or reveals there is none — before budget burns. Value case precedes solution design.

Tempting because competitive intelligence sounds diligent, but competitors' deployments cannot supply this company's value case: their processes, baselines, and economics are theirs. Benchmarking in service of 'they are doing agents' launders the original tech-led rationale rather than replacing it.
principle: no architecture without a named value pillar, metric, and owner
relatedConcept: Value-pillar alignment is the architect's defense against technology-led initiatives that consume budget without a measurable case.
overallExplanation: No architecture without a named value pillar, metric, and owner. Value-pillar alignment is the architect's defense against technology-led initiatives that consume budget without a measurable case.

objective: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
question: An education publisher has always sold static textbooks. Using Claude, it launches a service that generates an individualized practice curriculum for each student from that student's own errors and pace — something no amount of editorial staffing could produce, and now its fastest-growing revenue line. The board asks the architect to characterize the value pillar in the annual technology review. Which framing is correct?
options: Transformation, because the system creates a capability and revenue stream that did not and could not exist in the prior operating model
Productivity, because the editorial team now effectively serves every student individually instead of producing one shared textbook
Efficiency, because generating curricula by model is vastly cheaper per student than any manual authoring process would be
Cost, because the marginal cost of serving each additional student is near zero once the generation system is in place
optionExplanations: Correct. Transformation is the pillar for genuinely new capabilities and revenue — the stem states individualized curricula were impossible under the old model and now constitute a growing revenue line. Framing it correctly matters: transformation initiatives are judged on new revenue and capability metrics, not on cost-per-unit comparisons.

Tempting because 'editors serving every student' is a poetic reading, but productivity means existing people accomplishing more of their work; the editors' work has not scaled — an entirely new product exists that no editorial process produced. This mislabels a new capability as an amplification of the old one.

The cheaper-than-manual comparison is hypothetical: no manual process ever produced individualized curricula, so there is no baseline being beaten. Efficiency requires the same work done cheaper or faster; comparing against work that could never have been done misapplies the pillar.

Tempting because near-zero marginal cost is a real and attractive property, but it describes the economics of delivering the new capability, not the pillar the initiative serves. Leading the board with a cost framing undersells — and mismeasures — a revenue-creating transformation.
principle: transformation is a new capability or revenue stream, not a cheaper version of old work
relatedConcept: Distinguishing transformation from efficiency and productivity determines how an initiative is measured, funded, and defended.
overallExplanation: Transformation is a new capability or revenue stream, not a cheaper version of old work. Distinguishing transformation from efficiency and productivity determines how an initiative is measured, funded, and defended.

objective: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
question: A SaaS vendor's Claude-drafted support responses cost $0.42 per ticket against a mandated ceiling of $0.15, with quality above target. Analysis shows 70% of tickets are simple and short, while 30% are complex; every ticket currently gets the same Sonnet pipeline with the full knowledge base stuffed into each prompt's context. The architect must hit the ceiling without breaching the quality floor. What is the strongest approach?
options: Negotiate the ceiling up to $0.25 by presenting the quality metrics, since the mandated number predates evidence of what quality costs
Keep the pipeline but truncate the stuffed knowledge base to its most-used third, cutting input tokens roughly proportionally across all tickets
Move all tickets to Haiku immediately, which arithmetically lands under the ceiling, and accept whatever quality change follows
Route the simple 70% to Haiku, retrieve only relevant knowledge-base sections per ticket instead of stuffing everything, and reserve Sonnet for the complex 30%
optionExplanations: Tempting because the quality evidence is real, but the ceiling is stated as a mandate — a design constraint, not an opening bid — and the stem shows obvious architectural waste (uniform model, stuffed context) that has not been addressed. Negotiating before engineering asks the business to pay for the architecture's slack.

Blunt truncation cuts tokens but severs it from relevance: the discarded two-thirds is exactly what some tickets need, so quality degrades unpredictably on those. Retrieval achieves the same token reduction while preserving relevance — truncation is the crude version of the right idea.

Tempting because the arithmetic works, but 'accept whatever quality follows' abandons the stated quality floor on the 30% of complex tickets that plausibly need Sonnet. Uniform downgrade repeats the original design's error — treating heterogeneous tickets homogeneously — in the opposite direction.

Correct. This attacks both cost drivers in proportion to the workload's actual shape: model tiering matches capability to ticket difficulty, and per-ticket retrieval replaces paying for the whole knowledge base on every request. Cost targets are met by removing spend that buys no quality — the cost pillar served without sacrificing the floor.
principle: hit cost targets by matching model tier and context size to each request's actual needs
relatedConcept: Cost-pillar alignment turns a unit-economics target into specific architectural levers: tiering, routing, and retrieval scope.
overallExplanation: Hit cost targets by matching model tier and context size to each request's actual needs. Cost-pillar alignment turns a unit-economics target into specific architectural levers: tiering, routing, and retrieval scope.
